newsitem.title: GERMANY: UK must act before beef ban can be eased - Fischler.
newsitem.headline: UK must act before beef ban can be eased - Fischler.

text.p: The export ban on British beef could only start to be eased if Britain showed it was meeting necessary pre-conditions, Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler told a news conference on Thursday.
"It is up to Britain to show the additional cull (of 100,000 cattle, announced last month) is being implemented," he said.
He is in Berlin for the German "Green Week" agricultural fair.

British farm minister Doulgas Hogg plans to present poposals early in 1997 to exempt certified herds from the ban, imposed last March after London disclosed that mad cow disease (BSE) could be transmitted to humans.
Uncertainties persist about the cause of the disease and how to eradicate it.
Fischler said "certain consequences" were necessary after a draft European Parliament committee of inquiry report on Tuesday attacked Britain and the Commission for mishandling the crisis.
He said it would be wrong to designate scapegoats and dismiss them, but the Commission needed to divide legislation and check on its implementation more clearly.
He said he envisaged an independent body which would inform the public on a scientific basis about the steps taken by EU institutions to ensure food safety.

"I would wish that such an agency would develop a reputation similar to that of the (U.S.) Food and Drug Administration (FDA)," he said, but added he was aware meat markets did not come under FDA responsibility.
He said reform of EU farm policy must continue to prevent crises in various market segments and to embrace new member states in eastern Europe.
"We shouldn't be too hasty but we shouldn't maintain the status quo either," he told the news conference.

In 1999 at the latest the EU had to draw up new financial and structural plans in preparation for the new round of world trade talks and it needed to communicate to aspiring EU members details of the agricultural systems they would be joining.
"Only if we continue on this (reform) course, can we make demands on others," he said, alluding to U.S. and EU negotiations on competition in world food markets.

While the EU had successfully cut farm spending and output volumes, the crisis over mad cow disease and its possible human links had shown how fragile the EU farm system was and how quickly new costs and surpluses could arise, Fischler said.
He called the mad cow issue the "greatest crisis ever in the EU."

Negotiations with 10 applicants to join the EU would start in 1998 at the earliest, Fischler said. It was unlikely that they would join at the same date but there would be long transition periods, bridged by free trade agreements.
The eastern Europeans needed to restructure their inefficient farming systems and the EU would support this process with special transition funds.
Spain needed 12 years until full accession, he noted.

Fischler also said the EU must provide for when a "peace clause" allowing certain production-related farm payments ended in 2002. The EU must decouple these payments from output, for example by linking them to rural ecological services, to avoid massive pressure from competitors.
Fischler said the EU milk quota system needed to be reformed so that EU producers could compete in expanding world markets for milk and dairy products.
"Consumption in the EU will not rise and we need to export more -- but not with the help of massive subsidies," he said.
"We won't be able to operate without quotas, but they should be made more flexible."
The Commission is due to present a discussion paper on dairy reform, the most prominent EU farm topic apart from beef, before an informal farm ministers meeting at the end of May.
The current quota system expires at the end of March 2000.
Fischler said the quota system not only regulated production but also preserved dairy farming in structurally weak regions.
But the practice of leasing or selling unused allocations had distorted the system as it subsidised non-active dairy farmers and penalised others by inflating milk prices.
Fischler did not directly advocate milk price cuts, but said quota cuts alone would not help stabilise prices.
Instead, they would prevent the EU from exporting and pave the way for more imports.
